passage: I'm Wasim, and I sit opposite Sonali at work. At lunch Sonali was scrolling through a clip of a woman shouting at a shop clerk, with thousands of comments calling for her to be sacked and shamed. I watched Sonali type a comment, stare at it and delete it. Twice. Then Sonali said, "It's thirty seconds. What happened before?" and spent the rest of the break searching. A longer video turned up: the clerk had been curt for several minutes, and the woman was holding a crying child. Neither looked like the villain of a thirty-second clip. Sonali closed the app and posted nothing. I can't say what was in Sonali's mind, but the face looked tired, not angry.

qa.q: How long was the clip Sonali first saw?
qa.a: The clip was thirty seconds.

qa.q: What might Sonali have felt when typing and deleting the comment, and how sure can Wasim be?
qa.a: Pulled to join in but uneasy about it; Wasim only saw the typing and deleting and cannot be sure of Sonali's mind.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that was fair, and what could follow?
qa.a: Sonali looked for the earlier part and posted nothing, and could also decline to share the clip.

qa.q: How might the woman in the clip feel about thousands of comments?
qa.a: Humiliated and afraid, especially since her holding a crying child was missing from the short clip.

grounding: A user watches thousands attack a person over a clip, feels the pull to join, and refuses to add cruelty.

Monday. A clip of a man arguing with a bus conductor spread across every feed. By evening there were tens of thousands of comments demanding that the man lose his job. Sonali typed, "People like this should be..." then stopped, thumb hovering. She put the phone face down.
Wednesday. Siddharth from the next desk showed her a longer video: the fare dispute had run for ten minutes, and both men had raised their voices. Sonali felt relieved she had not posted.
Friday. Another clip trended. Sonali scrolled past, then messaged Siddharth: "Waiting for the full story this time." Siddharth wrote back, "Same."

qa.q: How many comments were there by Monday evening?
qa.a: There were tens of thousands of comments.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling while the thumb hovered over the comment?
qa.a: Tempted and uneasy; the pull to join the crowd met a doubt about adding cruelty.

qa.q: What did Sonali do differently on Friday?
qa.a: Sonali scrolled past the new clip and decided to wait for the full story.

qa.q: How might the man in the clip feel about the flood of comments?
qa.a: Exposed and frightened, since people demanded he lose his job while the longer video showed both men raising their voices.

grounding: A user feels the pull to join a pile-on, then sees the story was partial and refuses to add cruelty.

passage: Gopika, you asked why I never comment on those viral videos. Let your Hansa ma'am, the old hand at this desk, tell you. I was twenty-five, a trainee like you. A clip went round of a bus conductor screaming at a young woman, and within an hour it had thousands of angry comments, his address, calls to get him fired. I felt it too, that burning pull. I typed something nasty. My finger was right there. Then my senior at the time said, "Wait for the full video." I didn't post. Two days later the longer clip came out: the woman had slapped a child and he was protecting the child. The man had already been suspended. His daughter was crying in a news interview. I think about her face often. Nothing I didn't write could hurt anyone.

qa.q: What did the longer clip show?
qa.a: The woman had slapped a child and the conductor was protecting the child.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling while typing the nasty comment?
qa.a: Hansa felt a burning pull of anger, the same outrage everyone else was sharing, and was close to posting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her senior saying "Wait for the full video" made her hold back; the full clip showed the story had been partial, so her restraint spared an innocent man more cruelty.

qa.q: How was the conductor affected by the pile-on?
qa.a: He was suspended, his address was shared, and his daughter cried in an interview, so thousands of comments caused real harm to him and his family.

grounding: It illustrates an onlooker who feels the pull to join an online pile-on over a clip, holds back, and later learns the story was partial.

passage:
The flight to Kochi was delayed four hours and the gate was deafening, a cleaning machine on one side, a crying baby on the other. Jomon scrolled to pass the time. A clip was everywhere: a woman in a car park shouting at a delivery rider. Twenty-three thousand comments. Some shared her office name. His colleague Gurleen messaged: "Did you see this?? Disgusting. Tag her office." His thumb twitched. He felt that hot pull, the satisfaction of joining in.
Then he noticed the clip began mid-sentence. He watched it again with the sound up over the noise. Someone off-camera was also shouting. There was no start, no reason given.
He typed back, "Don't know what happened before. Not going to tag anyone." Gurleen sent an eye-roll. Jomon closed the app and bought tea. The board changed again: another hour.

qa.q: How long was the flight delayed at first?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: What did Jomon feel when Gurleen asked him to tag the office?
qa.a: He felt a hot pull and a kind of satisfaction at the thought of joining in, his thumb twitching.

qa.q: What did Jomon notice that helped him hold back?
qa.a: The clip began mid-sentence and someone off-camera was also shouting, so he realised he did not know the full story.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have seen Jomon's refusal?
qa.a: Gurleen seemed irritated or scornful, sending an eye-roll, perhaps feeling Jomon was avoiding taking a side.

grounding: It illustrates a user who feels the pull to join thousands attacking a person over a clip, sees the story is partial and refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
Sharmila was on the office shuttle in Pune when Thomas, her teammate, leaned across the aisle with his phone. "Look at this cab driver. Swearing at a passenger. Everyone's reporting him." The clip had half a million views. The comments were vicious: his number plate, his face circled, jokes about his accent. Sharmila felt the familiar itch. Her fingers were already forming a clever line. People would like it.
She watched it again. The clip was nine seconds long. The passenger was out of frame. Nobody knew what came before.
"You're not commenting?" Thomas asked.
"I don't know what happened," she said. "Neither does anyone in there."
Thomas shrugged. "He still swore."
"Maybe. Doesn't need my voice too." She put the phone in her bag and watched the traffic instead. It felt oddly lonely, and also like the right kind of quiet.

qa.q: How long was the clip?
qa.a: The clip was nine seconds long.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling as she read the comments?
qa.a: She felt a familiar itch, tempted to write a clever line people would like, before she stopped.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila's choice fair?
qa.a: She noticed the clip was short, the passenger was out of frame and nobody knew what came before, so she chose not to add to the cruelty.

qa.q: How does Thomas see the cab driver's clip?
qa.a: Thomas sees it as clear proof, saying "He still swore", and does not feel the need to know the rest of the story.

grounding: It illustrates an onlooker who feels the pull of an online pile-on, sees the story is partial, and quietly refuses to add cruelty.

passage:
"Have you seen this?" Deepika turned her laptop. A shaky clip: a woman at a petrol pump shouting at a young attendant. "Two million views. Everyone's calling her a monster. Someone's posted her office address."
Yash watched it twice. His thumb hovered over the reply box. He had a line ready, something sharp and funny. "She does look awful," he said.
"Wait," Deepika said. "Someone's put up a longer version." In the longer clip, the attendant had splashed fuel on the woman's child's shoes and laughed. The woman still shouted too much. But it was a different story.
"So what now? Do we defend her?" Yash asked.
"We don't have to do anything. That's the point. She's getting threats over thirty seconds."
Yash deleted his line. "Feels strange to just not."
"It's the most useful thing we can do."

qa.q: How many views did the clip have?
qa.a: The clip had two million views.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling as his thumb hovered over the reply box?
qa.a: Yash felt the pull to join in, excited by a sharp, funny line and carried along by the crowd's anger.

qa.q: Why was deleting his line a quiet act of fairness?
qa.a: The longer clip showed the story was partial, and not adding to thousands of attacks avoided more cruelty toward someone already being threatened.

qa.q: How might the woman in the clip be experiencing the pile-on?
qa.a: She is likely frightened and overwhelmed, with her office address out and threats pouring in over thirty seconds of her worst moment.

grounding: It illustrates a user who watches a pile-on over a clip, feels the pull to join, sees the story is partial and refuses to add cruelty.
